In a typical commercial surveillance system, such as the one illustrated here, video footage captured by security cameras in the field is transmitted and recorded by a gateway appliance, which could be either a network video recorder (NVR) or server.

This video data can just be stored in the gateway appliance, or optionally (and additionally) be stored in the cloud. Video Management System (VMS) and video analytics software could reside on the gateway appliance and/or the cloud.

First to market and leading the way in smart video surveillance

CCTV and smart video surveillance systems generate continuous video streams that demand storage built for 24/7 operation. Unlike standard desktop hard drives, surveillance-class drives are purpose-built to manage high write workloads, reduce frame loss, and operate reliably in challenging environments—such as outdoor enclosures or industrial installations.

If you're wondering about the difference between surveillance and desktop HDDs, it comes down to durability and performance. Desktop drives are designed for intermittent use and lighter workloads, while surveillance drives like WD Purple and WD Purple Pro are optimized for constant video recording across multiple streams.
WD Purple and WD Purple Pro drives offer:
Optimized performance for multi-camera CCTV and NVR setups
Resistance to high temperatures and humidity
Health monitoring (when used in compatible systems)

AI in Surveillance is called AI Video Analytics. Pattern recognition in frames of the video stream. In the past, this was simple 'line crossing' events, which were basic motion detection. Movement is detected in regions from one frame to the next. In the past several years, this has evolved into object detection. Not only is motion detected, but the object is recognized as a person, package, pet, vehicle, etc. This processing is happening on NVR recorders, which uses WD Purple HDDs. It happens on the back-end cloud on Ultrastar HDDs. While some AI video analytics are processed and saved inside the camera itself, some systems are also verified at the recorder or in the cloud on HDD storage.

The amount of storage your CCTV system requires depends on several factors — including camera resolution (e.g., 1080p, 4K, 8MP), video compression, frame rate, number of cameras, and how long you need to retain footage.

To make this easier, we offer a powerful and easy-to-use CCTV storage calculator. It helps you quickly estimate how much storage you’ll need for your specific setup — whether you're planning a small business installation or a large-scale, multi-site deployment.
Use our CCTV surveillance storage calculator to plan with confidence and ensure uninterrupted video retention.

The length of time you should store security video footage depends on your organization’s needs and compliance requirements. Most businesses retain footage for 30 to 90 days, but certain industries—such as financial services, healthcare, or public sector—may require longer retention periods due to regulatory guidelines.
To help plan your system, you can use our Surveillance Capacity Calculator. It lets you specify your retention period, number of cameras, resolution, and more to estimate the storage you’ll need.

A good rule of thumb is to follow the 3-2-1 rule: at least 3 copies of critical data, saved to at least 2 different media destinations, at least 1 of which is offsite. Thus, local backup can be a part of following data best practices by always backing up your data in multiple locations.

Workload Rate is defined as the amount of user data transferred to or from the hard drive. Workload Rate is annualized (TB transferred ✕ (8760 / recorded power-on hours)). Workload Rate will vary depending on your hardware and software components and configurations.

First used in the mid 1990s, it is less efficient and is likely the more common standard for lower resolution video. H.264, also known as Advanced Video Coding (AVC), was introduced in 2003 and is an efficient video compression standard commonly used for HD video (720p and 1080p) and Blu-Ray discs. H.265, also known as High Efficiency Video Coding (HEVC), was introduced in 2013 and is the latest video compression standard to be supported by newer NVRs, especially for 4K video support. Before selecting H.265, make sure that your DVR/NVR system supports this standard. H.265+ is an enhancement of H.265 that slightly improves the compression effectiveness. Some systems offer a separate H.265+ setting. Before selecting H.265+, make sure that your DVR/NVR system supports this setting.
